text.p: Twenty-year-old Tiger Woods rocked the golf world by rounding up a staggering $60 million in endorsement deals after turning pro two months ago.
Early results suggest golf's hottest property will not take long to prove he is worth it.
"Tiger is the greatest thing that's happened to the tour in a long time," said an admiring Payne Stewart, a former U.S. Open champion who finished second to Woods at last week's Disney World Classic.
The triumph was Woods's second tour title in three weeks and gave him a spot in the elite Tour Championship at Tulsa's Southern Hills, based on his winnings of $734,794 from just seven tournaments.
"The phones are ringing off the hook in Tulsa right now because Tiger is in the Tour Championship and people want to see him," said PGA Tour Commissioner Tim Finchem.
Sponsors have had their faith in the dynamic Woods confirmed as the three-time U.S. Amateur champion has moved spectacularly from Stanford University undergrad to pro superstar.
Woods has posted five straight top-five finishes by using his awesome length off the tee to turn challenging par fives into child's play, displaying touch and creativity around the greens.
Besides his special gifts as a player, Woods brings his own special brand of charisma to the sport.
Half African American and half Thai, the animated Woods is seen by many as a star who can shatter the lily white, country-club image ingrained in the game.
"Tiger has had a positive impact on the overall structure of the tour," says Finchem. "He's attracting more fans, many new fans to golf, raising interest in the sport.
"It's difficult to quantify his impact at this juncture but he has definitely changed the overall atmosphere and texture of the tour."
The end of the season has traditionally seen a slump in interest on the tour as the NFL season revs up and baseball's World Series gets under way.
Woods has changed all that this year.

"Clearly this fall, in terms of late tournament revenues from increased ticket sales, merchandise and food and beverage sales, he's had a tremendous impact and it seems to have grown as he's done better and better," Finchem said.
Stewart said: "He has brought incredible attention to golf at a time of year when football and the World Series always take precedence. Everything I've heard about him seems to be true."
Woods has had the magic touch and appeal for some time.
During the Amateur this year Woods wore a baseball cap decorated with the championship logo and the pro shop and merchandise tents sold out of that model almost immediately.
Since he turned pro, his sponsor's apparel has been selling at record levels at PGA Tour events.
When Woods won for the first time at the Las Vegas Invitational he used a limited edition Scotty Cameron putter, which had sold for $900.
After Woods's victory the putter was immediately priced as high as $10,000 among collectors.
Woods is on an incredible roll, vaulting into 14th place in the U.S. Ryder Cup team standings.
He would lead the tour in scoring (average 69.27 shots), driving distance (302.8 yards) and birdies (4.68 per round) if he had played enough to be eligible for statistical rankings.
Said fellow tour player Paul Goydos: "Tiger is like John Daly but with total control. If that's not a scary prospect for the rest of us, I don't know what is."
